# Linux essentials {#sec-linux}

::: {.tldr}
The minimum Linux for cluster work: move around the filesystem, edit files, find things,
inspect job output, and keep work alive when your connection drops with `tmux`.
:::

If you already live in a terminal, skim the `tmux` section. Everything here is standard
Linux; nothing is ARCC-specific except the paths.

## Moving around

```bash
pwd                 # where am I?
ls -lh              # list files, human-readable sizes
cd /project/cowy-firesurro   # go somewhere
cd                  # go home ($HOME)
cd -                # go back to where you just were
```

Three shortcuts you'll use constantly: `~` is your home directory, `.` is "here", and `..`
is "up one". Press <kbd>Tab</kbd> to complete a half-typed path.

## Looking at files without opening them

```bash
cat file.txt          # dump a whole (small) file
less big.log          # page through a big file; q to quit, / to search
head -n 20 file       # first 20 lines
tail -n 50 file       # last 50 lines
tail -f slurm-123.out # follow a job's output live as it's written
```

`tail -f` on a job's output file shows whether it's doing anything.

## Editing files

`nano` is the easy choice — arrow keys work, and shortcuts are listed at the bottom of the
screen (`^O` = save, `^X` = exit).

```bash
nano submit.sh
```

`vim` is powerful but has a learning curve; if you don't know it, `nano` is fine for a submit
script. For anything bigger, edit on your laptop and use the portal's file browser, VS Code's
Remote-SSH, or `rsync` (@sec-moving-data).

## Finding things

```bash
grep -r "account" .          # search file contents recursively
find . -name "*.nc"          # find files by name
find . -size +1G             # find files bigger than 1 GB (great for quota hunts)
du -sh *                     # how big is each thing in this directory?
```

`du -sh * | sort -h` finds what's eating your quota — useful given the 50 GB home limit
(@sec-storage).

## Environment variables and your shell

Your shell remembers settings in variables. A few you'll meet:

```bash
echo $HOME        # /home/<username>
echo $USER        # your username
echo $SCRATCH     # /gscratch/<username> — your scratch space
echo $PATH        # where the shell looks for commands
```

To make something permanent (say, a handy alias), add it to `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
alias q='squeue --me'          # see just my jobs
alias proj='cd /project/cowy-firesurro'
```

Run `source ~/.bashrc` (or log out and back in) to apply changes.

## `tmux`: keep work alive across a dropped connection {#sec-tmux}

When you SSH in and start something, **closing your laptop or losing WiFi kills that shell
and everything running in it.** `tmux` keeps your session alive on the login node whether or
not you're connected.

```bash
tmux new -s work     # start a named session "work"
#   ... do things, launch an interactive job, watch output ...
#   detach with:  Ctrl-b then d
tmux ls              # list your sessions
tmux attach -t work  # reattach later, even from a different computer
```

The workflow:

1. SSH into the login node.
2. `tmux new -s work`.
3. Inside tmux, do your editing, submit jobs, launch an interactive session (@sec-interactive).
4. Detach (<kbd>Ctrl-b</kbd> then <kbd>d</kbd>) and close your laptop. It all keeps running.
5. Tomorrow, SSH back in and `tmux attach -t work` — exactly where you left off.

::: {.callout-note}
## tmux is for login-node shells, not batch jobs
A batch job (`sbatch`, @sec-anatomy) already runs independently of your connection — log out
and it keeps going. `tmux` is for things that live in your shell: interactive sessions,
monitoring, an editor you don't want to lose.
:::

## Permissions, briefly

You'll occasionally see `chmod` and permission strings like `-rw-r-----`. The main uses are
fixing your SSH keys (`chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh`, from @sec-first-login) and making a script
executable:

```bash
chmod +x run.sh
```

There is **no `sudo` on the cluster**. You can't install system packages or change things
outside your own directories, and you don't need to — everything you install goes in your
own space (@sec-conda) or as modules (@sec-modules).
